rv.q: Easily one of the finest works of the decade, “Downstate” is the best new play I’ve seen since, well, “Downstate.”
Bruce Norris's shattering Downstate is hard to write about for the same reason it needs to be seen: It gives voice to the unspeakable.

A playwright’s responsibility isn’t to either forgive or condemn, but to render life in all its complexity, to present us with a vision of humanity that is truthful, as Mr. Norris so superbly does in this troubling but terrific play.

“Downstate,” bristling with ideas and distinguished by its refusal to offer comfort, is easily one of the most powerful plays I’ve seen this year, not despite but because of the fact that it left me wrung out and ready to argue for hours.

When you have a director and a cast who understands not only the complexity and causality of human feeling but also the impact of passing time, with its own pressures of forgiveness and the pressure to “move on,” you have something well worth your time.
Downstate dares us to forgive the unforgivable, challenging the very concept of grace.
Downstate forces us to stand at the shore of our own reservoir of mercy, to consider how deep it really goes.
Downstate is a blistering examination of what being treated as scum does to a person’s psyche.
Freeman, giving the performance of a lifetime as Dee, dominates "Downstate."
For those reasons, Bruce Norris’s daring play is a consummate work brilliantly presented in an immaculate production featuring some of the finest acting you’re likely to see on a Broadway stage.
Norris is the demolition expert of the American theater, giving audiences an up-close look as our simplistic fairy tales implode onstage.
I beg you not to avoid this remarkable work and production, which is currently the finest (and finest acted) show on Broadway!

Mantello’s production of the play is meticulously finished in every way, from designer Ann Roth’s character-true clothes to the way Heather Gilbert’s unobtrusive lighting design quietly suggests changes in mood.
Downstate, his most assured and hair-raising work to date, practically dares the audience to reject his four protagonists, a quartet of sex offenders drawn to the underage.

Although it's a show I don't particularly want to see again, Downstate is the kind of show at which repeat viewings would spark deeper thought about its complex debates and uncover new intricacies of the ensemble's layered performances.
The best play of 2022 is now the best revival to appear on Broadway in 2026.
Brought to life correctly, as it mostly is in this riveting new Broadway staging, it lands like a sledgehammer.
If the Off-Broadway production was superbly acted and directed, the Broadway version is even better.
Bruce Norris’ provocative drama gets a gripping Broadway revival that challenges easy judgments and stirs uncomfortable questions.
All in all, Downstate remains a play worth seeing (there isn’t another one like it) and Mantello’s production is finely calibrated.
Bruce Norris turns society’s most abhorred men into uneasy and unforgettable Broadway theater.
Downstate is a carefully constructed play that allows us to get a glimpse of life among a group of men whom society generally deems to be monsters.
Downstate does what only great theater can do: shed light on even the darkest, most abject corners of human existence.
If you’re made of stronger stuff, hold on tight: theatre doesn’t get much better than this.
On those merits, this is exceptional theatre.

Norris brings anger, denial, compassion, and arguments that resist comfortable answers into that house, creating a harrowing theatrical experience that asks us to consider the uneasy space between accountability and the possibility of understanding.
Downstate earns every squirm by making the men we’d rather not see disturbingly recognizable.
Seen together, the two plays make a similar demand: that we recognize the humanity of people whose acts we abhor without mistaking recognition for absolution.
The show is worth seeing because it reminds us of the power and importance of complexity.

By the end of the play, the audience at my performance seems to be on Norris’ wavelength, finding the sweet spot of comedy and tragedy of the play’s situation that I unfortunately still could not locate.

cn.t: Critics hail *Downstate* as a daring, essential Broadway achievement—Bruce Norris's tragicomedy about sex offenders in a group home unsettles and provokes in equal measure, with standout performances and direction earning near-universal praise.

lo.t: Opens 12 AM day before performance, closes 3 PM day before. Winners drawn at 10:00 AM and 3:00 PM.
lo.inst: Submit online form. Winners notified by email and have five hours to claim and purchase tickets online. Limit 2 tickets per person.

sg.ra: Expect a more partial view from the sides than from the center.
All eight rows are directly in line with the stage and provide elevated sightlines. Choose Rows A or B for some of the theater's best detailed views.
Choose inside seats in rows A or B for the cleanest and most detailed side-mezzanine views. Avoid double-digit seats by the far aisle if you want the least angled view.

sn.c: In Orchestra row O, the Mezzanine overhang cuts into the stage slightly.
sn.sh: Overhang cuts into the stage slightly

sn.c: Orchestra rows AA-BB may be too close to the stage for shorter theatergoers.
sn.sh: May be too close for shorter theatergoers

sn.c: The Boxes sit raised at the sides of the Orchestra. They are private, but the view of the stage is only partial.
sn.sh: Private, but only a partial view

sn.lo: Center Mezzanine, rows G to H
sn.c: Center Mezzanine rows G-H have an elevated and impressively detailed view of the stage for much less than the premium price.
sn.sh: Detailed views for less than premium

sn.c: Legroom can be quite tight in the Mezzanine. An aisle seat, especially near the center, gives extra space.

vs.sum: The Booth Theatre offers good sightlines with a well-raked mezzanine and clear views from most seats, though legroom can be tight. The theater's elegant, European-inspired design adds to its charm, while sound quality is consistently praised. Facilities are average, with typical restroom and concession offerings.

acc.note: 6 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Not completely wheelchair accessible. Infrared devices available.

vr.q: So if you like great theater, thought-provoking theater, then you have to go see Downstate.
